video.title: First programs: print, variables and input
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph at a staffroom table on a Friday afternoon, a pile of test papers, a calculator and a mark book. He taps the calculator, frowns at a smudged average, then holds up his phone.
scenes.animation: Calculator keys flash; a wrong average gets a red circle; the phone slides in.
scenes.narration: Every term I average two test marks for forty pupils, on a calculator. One slip, and a pupil gets the wrong mark. This term my phone does it, with four lines of Python.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and the Programming track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: your first Python programs, with print, variables and input.

scenes.visual: A code card types three print lines; an arrow runs down the left edge, line by line, and each message appears on a phone screen in turn.
scenes.animation: Lines type in; the arrow steps down one line at a time.
scenes.on_screen_text: One line at a time, top to bottom
scenes.narration: A program is a list of exact instructions. Python runs them one line at a time, from the top down. Here, print shows each message on the screen, in this order. Swap two lines, and the messages swap too.

scenes.visual: Two lines on a code card: the same sum with and without quotes. Under each, what the screen shows: the text 7 * 6, then 42.
scenes.animation: The second line lights up; 42 pops out beside it.
scenes.narration: Now look at the quotes. With quotes, Python shows the text exactly as you typed it. Without them, it works the sum out first. So the first line shows seven times six, and the second shows forty-two.

scenes.visual: A code card: two marks stored in variables, their average worked out, then printed. The names glow as they are used.
scenes.animation: Each line types in; the third line is highlighted as the narrator explains it.
scenes.on_screen_text: A variable: a name for a value
scenes.narration: A variable is a name that holds a value. The equals sign stores it: the value on the right goes into the name on the left. Then you can use the name, and Python uses its value. Here the average of fourteen and eighteen is sixteen.

scenes.visual: A shelf of labelled boxes. A box labelled “mark” holds 14; a hand takes the 14 out and puts in 15. The label stays.
scenes.animation: The old value slides out, the new one drops in.
scenes.narration: Think of a variable as a labelled box on a shelf. The label stays; what’s inside can change. Put a new value in, and the old one is gone. So a variable holds one value at a time.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma, one eyebrow raised, holds up a card with one line of code. Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! I print five in quotes, plus three in quotes. What appears on the screen?

scenes.visual: The card “53” gets a check badge. A code card shows the two lines side by side with their results as comments.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the comments type in.
scenes.narration: Fifty-three. In quotes, five and three are text, and plus joins text together, like two words. Without quotes, five plus three is eight. Text or number: Python always needs to know which.

scenes.visual: A code card with input: the program asks for a name and a mark, then prints them. A phone screen shows the questions and a pupil’s typed answers.
scenes.animation: The prompt blinks; typed answers appear; the int() line is highlighted.
scenes.on_screen_text: input() asks, and gives back text
scenes.narration: To ask a question, use input. The program waits, and whatever is typed comes back as text, even a number. To do sums with it, turn it into a whole number with int. Now my program can ask for any pupil’s marks.

scenes.visual: Four small tiles: a class average, a printed times table, a pass count with ticks, a phone with no signal still running Python.
scenes.animation: Tiles arrive one by one as they are named.
scenes.on_screen_text: A tool for your own work
scenes.narration: Small programs like this save teachers real time. Averages for a whole class. A times table to print for Primary Three. How many pupils passed. And it all runs on your phone, offline, in the same Python that runs on a micro:bit.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with the lab: a short program, a Next button, and a table of variables filling in as each line runs.
scenes.animation: A finger taps Next; a row in the variables table lights up each time.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: step through a program
scenes.narration: In the app, open Step through a program. Type your own lines, press Run and record, then Next: watch each variable appear as its line runs. Try two marks and their average.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up his phone showing “Mark? 12”. Three answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A pupil types twelve when my program asks for a mark. What does input give back?

scenes.visual: The text card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into four summary lines and an orange takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in 250 ms apart; the takeaway bar slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Top to bottom · Quotes make text · = stores · input gives text
scenes.narration: Text, so use int before any sums. Remember: Python runs top to bottom, one line at a time. Quotes make text. The equals sign stores a value in a variable. And input always gives text.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph’s classroom: three short programs on the board, pupils in pairs writing predictions, then Mr Joseph runs them on his phone and reads out the results.
scenes.animation: Predictions pop up on paper; ticks and crosses appear after the run.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: Predict, then run. Write three short programs on the board. Pairs write down what each one will show. Then run them on your phone and read out the results: who was right, and why?

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — in quotes, 5 and 3 are text, and + joins text: 53.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — in quotes, 5 and 3 are text, and + joins them like two words: 53. Without quotes it would be 8.

checkpoints.prompt: A pupil types 12 at input("Mark? "). What comes back?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — input always gives text. Turn it into a number with int() before any sums.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — input always gives back text, even when it looks like a number. Use int() before any sums.
